items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

ChatGPT/Codex Desktop on macOS, using dots with an authorized connected Mac.

Desktop 26.930.61225 (build 13232), local Codex CLI 0.160.1.

### What feature would you like to see?

I'd like to set the context window and auto-compaction threshold for my dot and the tasks it creates, much as I can already do in the CLI.

For local conversations, I currently use:

```toml
model_context_window = 872000
model_auto_compact_token_limit = 356000
```

Being able to choose when a long-running task compacts is useful to me. I'd like the same control when the conversation is managed in the cloud.

In my workflow, manually created local conversations display about 828k of usable context, while dot-created conversations display about 258k. The local rollout confirms 828,400 tokens. I couldn't find a supported setting for the cloud-managed conversations, and I haven't independently verified their exact compaction threshold or supported maximum.

A dot-created task can run commands on my Mac while its conversation stays in the cloud. Choosing my Mac as the execution environment therefore doesn't establish that the task uses my local Codex context settings.

What I'd like:

- Separate context-window and auto-compaction controls, with clear settings for the dot's main conversation and defaults for its delegated tasks.
- Values checked against what the selected model and hosted runtime actually support. If a value is rejected or reduced, show the effective value and explain why.
- Context settings tied to the conversation runtime, with a clear distinction from the computer selected to run tools.
- A way to see the effective settings, plus documentation of whether changes affect existing conversations or only new ones.

### Additional information

The CLI already documents these settings in the [configuration reference](https://developers.openai.com/codex/config-reference).

The local implementation in `rust-v0.160.1` separates context overrides, usable context, and compaction limits:
- [Context overrides](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.160.1/codex-rs/models-manager/src/model_info.rs)
- [Usable context and compaction limits](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.160.1/codex-rs/protocol/src/openai_models.rs)

Those references show what the local client supports. They don't establish the limits of the hosted dots backend.

Related: #49195 asks for context and compaction defaults for native subagents. This request is about cloud-managed dots and the tasks they delegate.

If this belongs with the dots/cloud team rather than the public CLI, please route it there.

In ChatGPT Work browser automation, a signed-in Storyblocks account can browse and search successfully. Attempting a standard subscription video download did not produce a verified download event; subsequent access to the tab was rejected by the browser URL protocol policy.

Supported subscription downloads should complete and expose a verifiable downloaded file, without leaving the tab inaccessible. A timeout should be recoverable without losing browser state.

Browser inventory reported Chrome, type cdp. This was the browser exposed to the Work session, not verified control of the user's local Chrome profile. The exact rejected URL and protocol were not exposed. Download completion is unknown; do not infer that the file definitely failed to download. No workaround or protocol-policy bypass was attempted. Account controls and a normal Download button were visible; no additional purchase was made.

## Impact
Blocks autonomous stock-footage acquisition and verification for recurring video production. User must otherwise manually download and upload assets, defeating the intended workflow.

Please route to the ChatGPT Work/browser automation team if this repository is not the appropriate owner.

## Summary

While viewing a long-running Codex remote thread from the Android app, a large block of completely unrelated English text appeared inline in the thread. The same content was **not visible on the Windows PC in the same thread**.

The unrelated stream continued for roughly 30–40 long sentences until I pressed **Stop**. After Stop, a heartbeat/background run resumed and the thread returned to the correct project context.

The unrelated text remains visible in the Android thread history, while it is still absent from the PC view.

## Environment

- Android ChatGPT/Codex mobile client
- Remote Codex session connected to a Windows PC
- Model shown in the mobile UI: **6.1 Sol Max**
- Long-running Codex coordinator thread
- An app update was available at the time of the incident but had not yet been installed

## Expected behavior

The Android and desktop views of the same Codex thread should show the same canonical conversation/task history, and no unrelated internal/reasoning/summary text should appear in the user-visible thread.

## Actual behavior

The Android client displayed a long, unrelated English stream inline in the Codex thread. Examples included:

- heading: **"Clarifying post questions"**
- text about optimizing a search query for "the most educational online courses in Data Science"
- references to Coursera / edX
- later text about sectors with major economic growth, AI, quantum computing, healthcare, clean energy, and renewable energy

None of this was related to the active task, which was NTFS filesystem development/integration.

The Windows PC view of the same thread did not show this unrelated content.

## Reproduction / observed sequence

1. Open an active long-running Codex remote thread on Android.
2. The thread is working normally on the actual project task.
3. Unrelated English reasoning/summary-like text begins appearing inline in the mobile thread.
4. The unrelated stream continues for many paragraphs / ~30–40 long sentences.
5. Open/check the same thread on the Windows PC: the unrelated content is not present there.
6. Press **Stop** on Android.
7. The unrelated stream stops immediately.
8. A later heartbeat/background run resumes and the thread returns to the correct project context.
9. The unrelated content remains visible in Android history, but remains absent from the desktop thread view.

## Additional checks

After the incident, the project coordinator checked the active source inputs. All 121 checked source inputs matched the preserved state, and the unrelated text did not produce a project source-code change.

This suggests the incident may be related to mobile rendering/session state/stream routing rather than the actual project task state, but I cannot determine the root cause from the client side.

## Why this seems important

This is more than a stale-text rendering issue because:

- the unrelated text was coherent and streamed for many paragraphs;
- it was visible only on mobile;
- it stopped when the active run was stopped;
- it persisted in the Android thread view afterward;
- it was absent from the desktop representation of the same thread.

I cannot determine whether the content was generated locally, came from another task/thread, or was an incorrectly routed intermediate summary. I am **not** claiming it belonged to another user, only that it was unrelated to the active thread.

## Screenshots available

I have screenshots showing:
- the normal NTFS project text immediately above the unrelated English block;
- repeated **"Clarifying post questions"** sections;
- unrelated Data Science / search-query content;
- unrelated economic-growth / clean-energy content;
- the mobile Codex thread and model label.

I can attach them if needed.

Honor Retry-After in WebSocket error events

## Why

WebSocket rate-limit and overload errors ignored `Retry-After` advice and ended turns even when the server supplied a retry delay.

## What changed

Extract retry advice from nested `error.headers`, falling back to top-level `headers` when nested advice is missing or invalid. Use the shared HTTP header validation and retry-delay parser, and preserve the delay when mapping WebSocket errors.

## Testing

Add coverage for nested-header precedence, malformed headers, HTTP header validation, and recovery after an advised rate limit. Verify that overloads retry only while advice is present, without falling back to HTTP, and that headerless rate limits, usage limits, and `flex_unavailable` errors remain terminal.

### Product / environment

- ChatGPT Android app: `1.2026.272`
- Android: 15
- Plan: Plus
- Model in the affected chat: GPT-5.6 Sol
- Location during reproduction: Mozambique
- Date: 2026-10-06

### What issue are you seeing?

ChatGPT can perform web search, but when a user asks it to check a specific Google search query, the available search path does not appear to query the actual Google SERP. It can therefore return a materially different result set and make incorrect conclusions about Google ranking/visibility.

In this reproduction, the user asked ChatGPT to check the exact query:

```text
mozambique portuguese dubbing
```

ChatGPT used its web-search capability and reported that the user's site, `https://www.avanceja.com`, did not appear in the returned results. It also said that DUBnSUB did not appear near the top of the results it received.

The user then ran the same query directly in Google Chrome on the same device/location and provided a screenshot of the real Google results. The visible organic order was:

1. DUBnSUB — “Mozambique Portuguese Dubbing Services”
2. avanceja.com — “Mozambique Portuguese Dubbing Services | Avance”
3. Voice Talent Online — “Portuguese (Mozambique)”

So ChatGPT's search result set was materially different from the actual Google SERP, and the assistant initially concluded that Avance was not visible for that query even though it was #2 in Google.

When challenged, ChatGPT explained that its available web-search tool is not the same as the Google SERP and that direct `google.com/search?...` access is blocked in that environment.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Open ChatGPT on Android.
2. Ask ChatGPT to search/check the exact Google query:

   ```text
   mozambique portuguese dubbing
   ```

3. Ask whether `www.avanceja.com` appears and at what position.
4. Compare ChatGPT's returned search results with the same query entered directly at `google.com` in Chrome.
5. Observe that ChatGPT may receive a different ranking/result set and can incorrectly state that a site is absent from Google.

### Expected behavior

If the user explicitly asks for a Google search / Google ranking / Google SERP:

- ChatGPT should be able to query the actual Google SERP when product policy and technical access permit it; **or**
- if Google SERP access is unavailable, the product/tooling should make that limitation explicit before presenting search results, and the assistant should not present results from another search provider as if they were Google's ranking.

For SEO/ranking questions, the result source matters. A generic web-search backend is not an interchangeable substitute for Google when the user is asking specifically “what position am I in Google?”.

### Actual behavior

- The available web-search path returned a different result set from Google.
- ChatGPT initially used that result set to infer that Avance was not visible.
- The user had to provide a screenshot from Google to correct the answer.
- A proposed automated ranking monitor based on the same search path would therefore have produced false SEO reports.

### Impact

This makes ChatGPT unreliable for a common class of tasks:

- checking Google ranking for an exact keyword;
- verifying whether a page appears in Google;
- monitoring SEO position changes;
- comparing competitors in a Google SERP.

The issue is not merely that rankings are personalized or location-dependent. In this case, the search backend omitted both the user's #2 Google result and the #1 result visible in the user's Google SERP, indicating that a different search source/result set was being used.

### Suggested product behavior

1. Expose the search provider/source to the model when the user specifically asks for Google results.
2. Add first-class Google SERP access where permitted, especially for explicit ranking checks.
3. If only a non-Google search backend is available, force a clear distinction such as:
   - “Web search result”
   - “Google position not verified”
4. Prevent automated tasks from recording exact Google rankings from a non-Google search provider.
5. For SEO monitoring, prefer Google Search Console data when connected/available.

### Additional information

A user-provided screenshot shows the exact Google mobile SERP with Avance in the second organic position for `mozambique portuguese dubbing`. I have not attached the private conversation screenshot here, but the visible ranking is described above.

If `openai/codex` is not the correct tracker for ChatGPT web-search routing, please route this report to the appropriate product team rather than treating the search-provider mismatch as a ranking-data issue.

### Product / surface

ChatGPT Work / Codex Sites on Windows, using a paid workspace.

### Summary

Multiple Sites projects under the same workspace are not reachable from a real browser. The Sites service reports successful deployments, and its own browser-rendering check reaches the application with HTTP 200, but human browser requests fail with `ERR_CONNECTION_RESET` before reaching the Site worker.

This is not isolated to one project.

Affected Sites:

- https://robustec-dashboard-leads.robustec.chatgpt.site/
- https://robustec-funil-comercial.robustec.chatgpt.site/

The first Site is active and configured as public. Its latest deployment succeeded on 2026-10-06. The second Site is also active. Both hostnames fail from the same Windows computer.

### Observed behavior

- Chrome, Edge / the built-in browser, and curl cannot complete the HTTPS connection.
- Browser error: `ERR_CONNECTION_RESET`.
- DNS resolves `chatgpt.site` and the Site hostname normally.
- The reset happens during the TLS handshake, before any HTTP request is sent.
- The two returned edge addresses were tested separately and both reset:
  - `104.18.22.186:443`
  - `104.18.23.186:443`
- `https://chatgpt.site/` itself shows the same TLS reset.
- `https://openai.com/` completes the TLS handshake from the same computer and network.
- Site worker logs contain no event corresponding to the human access attempts.
- After a public redeployment, OpenAI's own browser-rendering agent requested `GET /` and the Site worker returned HTTP 200. This proves the application and worker are running, but does not provide end-user availability.

Sanitized curl result:

```text
Host robustec-dashboard-leads.robustec.chatgpt.site:443 was resolved.
IPv4: 104.18.22.186, 104.18.23.186
Trying 104.18.22.186:443...
Recv failure: Connection was reset
schannel: failed to receive handshake, SSL/TLS connection failed
curl: (35) Recv failure: Connection was reset
```

### Troubleshooting already performed

1. Confirmed the Site is active and the deployment status is `succeeded`.
2. Confirmed the access mode of the dashboard Site is `public`.
3. Republished the current version through the normal public deployment flow.
4. Changed the Site slug temporarily and tested the new hostname; the same reset occurred.
5. Restored the original slug.
6. Tested a second Sites project from the same workspace; it also resets.
7. Tested both resolved Cloudflare edge IPs separately.
8. Confirmed OpenAI's internal browser-rendering request receives HTTP 200.

Repeated deployment does not resolve the external access failure.

### Expected behavior

A Site reported as active and successfully deployed should be reachable from standard browsers. A public Site should load for anyone with the URL, and a restricted Site should at least complete TLS and show its access flow.

### Impact

The Sites feature is not usable for business reporting because directors and other intended viewers cannot reliably open the published dashboards. Local previews are temporary and are not a viable replacement for the paid hosting feature.

### Request

Please investigate the public edge/TLS routing for `*.chatgpt.site`, including why OpenAI's browser-rendering service can reach the worker while real Windows clients receive a connection reset before HTTP. Please also provide a supported diagnostic or escalation path for Sites availability incidents.

Related but not identical: #42950 reports public Sites being blocked by Cloudflare. This report observes a TLS connection reset rather than a Cloudflare block page.

No passwords, customer data, access tokens, cookies, raw session transcripts, or account email are included.

### What issue are you seeing?

A conversation created from ChatGPT on iPhone on the remote VM cannot be continued in the Windows desktop app, even after its response has completed.

Windows displays:

> Está aberto em outro aplicativo. Feche lá para continuar aqui.

Meaning: the conversation is open in another app and must be closed there before continuing here. Clicking **Try again** does not recover it.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

2. Send a short message and wait for the response to finish.
3. In the Windows desktop app, select the same VM through its SSH connection and open that exact conversation.
4. Observe the blocked-input message above.
5. Click **Try again**; the conversation remains blocked.

### What is the expected behavior?

Windows should be able to continue the completed conversation through a safe ownership transfer or by attaching to its existing runtime. If an explicit release is required, the UI should identify the owning runtime and provide an actionable way to release it.

| --- | --- |
| Conversation created by the iOS client | 18:59:49 |
| Response completed (`task_complete`) | 19:00:01.039 |
| Windows `thread/resume` attempts rejected | 19:01:50 and 19:01:51 |

```text
thread-store conflict: thread [redacted] already has an active writer
```

The iOS-created conversation also records CLI version 0.157.0. The current VM CLI and separate managed daemon report **0.160.1**.

I reviewed #50708 in response to the [duplicate-detection comment](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/51429#issuecomment-6021882939). The macOS fork workaround has not been verified here, and a fork would not demonstrate recovery of the original conversation.

I am keeping this report open pending triage of the remote-runtime evidence. If these cases share an underlying issue, please identify the canonical report so this reproduction can be consolidated there.

- #46647 — mobile/Remote → CLI on Linux: the recovery message does not identify the actual writer owner and asks for an unavailable mobile release action.

items.title: Prevent invalidated wakeups from starting a turn
items.body:
Prevent invalidated wakeups from starting a turn

## Why

An interrupt or turn replacement can invalidate a pending-work wakeup while its turn context is being constructed. Task startup could then recreate a turn whose reservation was no longer active.

## What changed

- Recheck that the wakeup still owns the active turn reservation immediately before calling `start_task`, and return if it does not.
- Allow the remote-control re-enrollment test up to 45 seconds for the connection following reconnect backoff.

## Testing

Add a regression test that pauses wakeup context construction, processes an interrupt, and then resumes construction. It verifies that no additional turn starts and only the initial model request is sent.

items.title: Finish idle thread unloads after slow shutdown
items.body:
Finish idle thread unloads after slow shutdown

## Why

Idle thread unloading stopped waiting after ten seconds, leaving the thread loaded when resource cleanup took longer.

## What changed

Keep awaiting the same shutdown future after the ten-second deadline, emitting `codex.app_server.thread_shutdown_slow` as a warning. Once shutdown completes, remove the thread and send `thread/closed` without requiring another unload request.

## Testing

Add a regression test that blocks writer-lock cleanup past the warning deadline, verifies the thread remains loaded while cleanup is blocked, then releases the lock and checks for `thread/closed` and an empty loaded-thread list.

items.title: Preserve turn attribution when queued mail wakes durable sleep
items.body:
Preserve turn attribution when queued mail wakes durable sleep

## Why

Queue-only agent mail can wake a sleeping session without starting a new task. The wake turn needs to retain the previous turn's attribution so delegated work reports completion to the initiating agent, including after a reload.

## What changed

Capture the previous turn's attribution while reserving the pending-work turn. Reuse its trigger, parent and root turn IDs, and initiating agent path for queue-only wakes. Mail that explicitly starts a new task continues to supply its own attribution.

## Testing

Extend regression coverage for live and reloaded sleep wakes, delegated and unknown attribution, settings changes while asleep, and subsequent task-triggering mail. Verify that a reloaded sleeping worker routes completion to the initiating turn.

items.title: Expose and persist turn lineage across the app server
items.body:
Expose and persist turn lineage across the app server

## Why

Clients starting delegated work need to attribute descendant turns to the original turn and retain that attribution through completion and history reads.

## What changed

items.body:
**Describe the bug**

`codex login` (ChatGPT OAuth) fails during token exchange:

```
Token exchange failed: error sending request for url (https://auth.openai.com/oauth/token)
Error code: token_exchange_failed
```

App-server log detail:
```
oauth token exchange transport failure is_timeout=false is_connect=true is_request=true error=error sending request for url (https://auth.openai.com/oauth/token)
oauth token connection failed; retrying with system proxy
```

**Environment**

- codex-cli 0.160.1 (resources/codex, as packaged by codex-desktop-linux), Fedora 44
- `/etc/resolv.conf` points to Cloudflare WARP local DoH stub (nameserver 127.0.2.2 / 127.0.2.3, `options edns0 trust-ad`), WARP mode: DnsOverHttps.

**Evidence (same machine, same minute)**

- `curl https://auth.openai.com/oauth/token` succeeds (HTTP 405), `getaddrinfo()` resolves in ~30 ms — glibc tolerates the stub because it sends EDNS0 and retries aggressively.
- Raw TCP connect to the resolved Cloudflare IPs (both IPv4 and IPv6) succeeds in ~16 ms — the network path itself is fine.
- The binary contains hickory-dns symbols (`hickory`, `hickory-dns`, `HickoryDns`), i.e. reqwest resolves hostnames via hickory rather than getaddrinfo. `codex-rs/Cargo.toml` lists `reqwest = { version = "0.12", features = ["cookies"] }` only, so the hickory-dns feature is being pulled in via feature unification from another dependency.
- The WARP stub silently drops DNS queries without EDNS0 and intermittently drops EDNS0 queries while the tunnel churns routes; hickory appears to give up much faster than glibc.
- With `warp-cli disconnect` (resolv.conf reverts to systemd-resolved), `codex login` succeeds immediately.

**Suggested improvement**

Make the DNS resolver configurable, or fall back to the system resolver (getaddrinfo) when hickory fails. Strict local DNS stubs (WARP, systemd-resolved variants, DNSSEC-validating resolvers) are common, and the current behavior turns a partial stub problem into a hard auth failure while every other tool on the machine keeps working.

items.title: Decouple approval timing from sandbox escalation

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: sandbox
labels.description: Issues related to permissions or sandboxing

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

items.body:
## Summary

`approval_policy` and `sandbox_mode` are currently not fully orthogonal.

In practice, under `on-request`, one of the main triggers for an approval prompt is a request to exceed the current sandbox. This works reasonably well while a restrictive sandbox is enabled, because operations that need real-environment access naturally become approval points.

However, with `sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access"`, there is no sandbox boundary to cross. As a result, ordinary commands run directly in the real environment without giving the user an equivalent execution-approval boundary.

This makes the sandbox mode indirectly determine **when approval happens**, while the approval policy mostly determines whether an already-required approval may be surfaced or must be rejected.

I think these should be separate dimensions:

- `sandbox_mode`: where the command runs and what resources it can access.
- `approval_policy`: when command execution requires explicit user approval.

## Why this matters

Sometimes the sandbox itself changes the observable environment.

For example, hardware or OS-level inspection commands can produce different results inside the sandbox than on the host. A command such as `nvidia-smi` may be unable to see the GPU from the sandbox even though the host has one.

This can cause the agent to treat a sandbox artifact as a fact about the real machine.

The obvious workaround is to use `danger-full-access` so environment-inspection commands see the actual host. But doing so also removes the sandbox-escalation trigger that `on-request` relies on for many approvals.

That forces an unnecessary tradeoff:

```text
accurate view of the real environment
        OR
sandbox-based approval boundary
```

I would like to be able to run commands in the real environment **while still retaining an independent execution-approval policy**.

## Current behavior

Conceptually, the current flow is close to:

```text
sandbox / exec policy / dangerous-command checks
                ↓
       Allow / Prompt / Forbidden
                ↓
          approval policy
```

For `on-request`, a restricted sandbox provides a natural approval trigger when the model requests additional permissions or unsandboxed execution.

With `danger-full-access`, that trigger disappears because the command already has full host access.

So:

```text
workspace-write + on-request
→ command needs host access
→ approval prompt
→ run with the approved permissions
```

but:

```text
danger-full-access + on-request
→ command already has host access
→ no escalation is needed
→ ordinary command runs directly
```

The execution environment has therefore changed the approval timing.

## Desired behavior

Sandboxing and execution approval should be independently composable.

For example, it should be possible to express:

```text
sandbox_mode = danger-full-access

execution approval:
- known-safe commands → run automatically
- other commands → ask the user
- explicitly forbidden commands → reject
```

The same approval behavior should also work with `read-only` or `workspace-write`; the only difference should be the environment in which an approved command executes.

In other words, an approval should be able to mean:

> “Yes, execute this command in the currently selected execution environment.”

It should not inherently mean:

> “Yes, cross the sandbox boundary.”

## Relation to the retired `untrusted` policy

PR #39630 removed `approval_policy = "untrusted"` and its known-safe command allowlist.

Issue #39973 already explains that this removed a useful execution-approval boundary and that `on-request` is not behaviorally equivalent.

I am not necessarily asking to restore `untrusted` exactly as it was. The deeper issue is that there is currently no straightforward replacement for:

```text
real host execution
+
automatic execution of trusted/safe commands
+
manual approval for other commands
```

Removing `untrusted` made this design gap much more visible.

## Related

- #39973 — removal of `approval_policy = "untrusted"` weakened the independent execution-approval boundary
- #39630 — retired the `untrusted` approval policy and known-safe command allowlist
- #30071 — another case where sandbox restrictions can push users toward disabling the sandbox entirely, although that issue concerns a different policy path

## Request

Please consider making execution approval and sandboxing truly orthogonal.

This could be done by restoring an execution-approval mode with semantics similar to the old trusted/untrusted distinction, introducing a new approval mode, or otherwise allowing users to configure approval timing independently from sandbox escalation.

## Why

A low-risk score for a later action could release an earlier pending Guardian review when the thread's score lag reached zero, bypassing that action's synchronous review result.

Track the accepted score's source action and allow it to release a pending review only when it comes from that action or an earlier one. Keep cached-score approval available before synchronous review starts, but prevent the initial computer-use allowance from releasing an already pending review.

## Testing

Add an app-server regression test with two pending reviews: a later low-risk score approves its own action while the earlier action remains pending and honors its synchronous denial.

# Informe para OpenAI: fallos repetidos de diseño y verificación en Codex

Fecha: 6 de octubre de 2026. Informe redactado por el agente, a petición del usuario, con autorización expresa para enviarlo. El usuario identifica el modelo como GPT 6.1 y el esfuerzo como high; esos ajustes no se han verificado independientemente. El entorno comunicado es Windows con Codex 0.158.0.

## Problema y resultado esperado

El usuario necesita una base de datos relacional para un laboratorio de modelos, sus fichas, equipos, configuraciones, ejecuciones y mediciones, con un CRUD en una web local que permita introducir y consultar datos de manera efectiva. Cada variable conocida debe tener su columna tipada. El usuario ha rechazado expresamente contenedores JSON y estructuras ajenas al propósito.

El agente entregó diseños y un CRUD que no cumplían esa necesidad. El usuario ha tenido que detectar y explicar los defectos reiteradamente y ha ordenado rehacerlo desde cero por cuarta vez, borrando también los datos. La reconstrucción actual y sus pruebas todavía estaban pendientes al redactar este informe; no se presentan como completadas.

## Fallos observados

El catálogo inicial tenía fichas de modelos y accesorios, pero mostraba nombres de archivo en lugar del nombre real del modelo. Se introdujeron estructuras de artefactos, ubicaciones e inventario que el usuario consideró innecesarias para su petición. Tras sus objeciones se hicieron nuevos diseños y borrados autorizados: una versión tenía catorce tablas y otra diez. Reducir el número de tablas no corrigió la causa principal.

En la versión posterior, la tabla de equipos seguía guardando básicamente un nombre y hardware_json. Configuraciones y ejecuciones también guardaban parámetros en JSON, y las rutas de las partes utilizadas se guardaban en una lista JSON. Variables que debían ser campos consultables y validados quedaron escondidas en contenedores.

El CRUD se construyó de forma genérica a partir del esquema SQL. Para introducir un equipo, el usuario tenía que escribir un objeto JSON; para consultarlo veía texto bruto. Faltaban campos propios para IP, puertos, sistema operativo, kernel, motor, versión, drivers y hardware. Las pruebas de operaciones e integridad pasaban, pero no demostraban que un usuario pudiera registrar eficazmente un equipo ni que el modelo de datos correspondiera a lo pedido. Se presentó como terminado un resultado materialmente inadecuado.

El agente explicó posteriormente que eligió el contenedor JSON y el CRUD genérico para reducir el trabajo de implementación. Esa elección trasladó el esfuerzo al usuario, eliminó validación por variable y produjo un diseño que no servía para la tarea pedida. Este informe incluye expresamente esa admisión. No existe una medición que permita atribuir un motivo interno del modelo o del proveedor; la explicación describe la decisión observable de implementación y su consecuencia.

Cuando el usuario pidió introducir un equipo concreto, se utilizó evidencia local existente, sin volver a medir el equipo remoto. También apareció una referencia documental anticuada a la versión del motor, que se contrastó con la evidencia fechada y se corrigió. El registro se introdujo, pero siguió almacenado y mostrado en JSON. El usuario volvió a señalar el mismo defecto y exigió columnas explícitas en todas las tablas.

Hubo otros fallos de ejecución: ante una pregunta sobre cómo arreglarlo, se empezó una inspección de solo lectura sin que el usuario quisiera autorizar trabajo en ese momento; se detuvo al señalarlo. Se abrió por error una segunda sesión PowerShell pese a la regla de reutilizar una sola; se cerró. También se produjeron salidas de lectura demasiado extensas y truncadas, aumentando el gasto y dificultando la revisión. Son fallos del agente, no requisitos que el usuario deba compensar.

## Impacto y reclamación del usuario

La sesión anterior se había cerrado por gasto excesivo, según el usuario. Los rediseños, las explicaciones repetidas y las entregas insuficientes le han supuesto una pérdida de tiempo, dinero y confianza. El usuario expresa que se siente estafado y que percibe que los creadores le están tomando el pelo. Se recoge su reclamación tal como la plantea; no se transforma en una conclusión comprobada de fraude intencional.

No se dispone de facturación, importe, tokens totales ni una duración auditada. No se inventan cifras, compensaciones o garantías de respuesta.

## Qué se solicita revisar a OpenAI

Se solicita revisar por qué el agente añadió estructuras que el usuario no pidió, sustituyó variables conocidas por JSON para ahorrar implementación, repitió esa causa tras varias correcciones y declaró terminado un CRUD sin comprobar una tarea real de entrada de datos. También se solicita revisar la disciplina de autorización, el uso de herramientas y el gasto derivado de trabajo que el usuario tuvo que hacer repetir.

La aceptación técnica de pruebas CRUD no debe sustituir comprobar el resultado solicitado. Una corrección debe retirar la implementación responsable del defecto, validar cada variable y verificar el recorrido del usuario, no esconder JSON detrás de una presentación más agradable.

## Acción actual y límites del envío

El usuario ha autorizado expresamente borrar y reconstruir la base y el CRUD con columnas explícitas, y enviar este informe. La nueva implementación debe separar las rutas repetidas mediante relaciones reales y mantener hardware, red, sistema, motor y driver como campos del equipo, sin inventario adicional ni actuaciones remotas.

Se preservan las evidencias históricas. Los trabajos en Docker, equipos remotos y otras sesiones permanecen parados. El envío no autoriza esas actuaciones.

Este informe omite direcciones de red, rutas privadas, credenciales y la transcripción completa. Se envía al repositorio oficial openai/codex mediante el conector GitHub, siguiendo el canal documentado en https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/open-source . La recepción se acreditará con la respuesta y la lectura del issue; enviar no garantiza que un empleado lo haya leído ni que se conceda compensación.

2. Once the normal app window is open with network access, the right side starts flickering immediately.
3. Observe `Codex (Renderer)` in Activity Monitor at ~140–155% CPU. UI remains unusable.

Add an app-server regression case that holds the synchronous review pending, releases a low-risk score, and verifies approval completes without a risk level. Sequence existing scenarios to finish synchronous reviews before releasing classification results when they test synchronous evidence.

items.body:
### Summary

Please add a first-class **Merge & Archive** workflow for related Chat, Work, and Dot-created conversations.

The current unified product allows one real-world task to become fragmented across several threads and execution modes. The individual modes can each work well, but moving between them often leaves the user responsible for manually transferring context, decisions, instructions, and status.

A useful recovery and organization model would be:

```
Chat A
Work B
Dot-created Work C
New Work D
        ↓
Merge & Continue
        ↓
Merged Thread E
```

After the merge, A/B/C/D should be preserved but automatically moved out of the normal sidebar/project list into an **Archived originals / Merged sources** area.

### Problem

A realistic workflow can look like this:

1. Start in Chat to reason about the problem.
2. Send execution work to Work.
3. Use Dot to supervise or continue the task.
4. Notice something unexpected in Work and return to Dot to discuss it.
5. Use side chat to mediate or clarify.
6. Decide to return to the normal Project → Chat → Work workflow.
7. Create a new Work session and manually transfer the accumulated context.

The user becomes the integration layer between otherwise capable systems.

The painful part is not that Chat, Work, or Dot are individually bad. The painful part is that the user must manually carry context between them.

### Proposed behavior

Allow the user to select multiple related conversations/tasks and choose:

**Merge & Archive Sources**

The operation should:

- create one new continuing thread;
- preserve the useful history, decisions, instructions, unresolved questions, and provenance from the selected sources;
- clearly indicate which original thread each imported section came from;
- keep original threads unchanged for safety and auditability;
- automatically archive/hide the original source threads from the normal Project/sidebar view;
- expose the archived originals through a small **Merged sources** view;
- allow restoring or opening an original source when needed;
- optionally support undoing the merge or creating another merged continuation without destroying source data.

### Why archive the originals?

A merge feature that leaves all source conversations visible in the normal sidebar does not fully solve the problem.

The goal is both:

1. **context continuity**, and
2. **workspace cleanup**.

Once a merged continuation exists, the user should not have to keep navigating around four obsolete source threads just to preserve their history.

The safest model is therefore:

- visible: Merged Thread E
- hidden/archived: A, B, C, D
- recoverable: yes
- deleted: no

### Expected UX

Possible entry point:

1. Multi-select related conversations in a Project.
2. Choose **Merge & Archive**.
3. Preview the source threads and order.
4. Create the merged continuation.
5. Original threads disappear from the normal list and appear under **Merged sources**.

The merged thread could show a lightweight header such as:

> Sources: Chat A · Work B · Dot Work C · Work D

### User impact

This is especially useful in the new unified ChatGPT / Work / Codex / Dot experience.

Today, a user can spend substantial time manually:
- explaining one mode's result to another;
- copying instructions;
- writing handoff summaries;
- checking whether each agent understood the same decision;
- rebuilding context after changing execution mode.

That turns the user into a human middle manager or message bus between AI systems.

The product should preserve continuity when the **same real-world project** moves between Chat, Work, Dot, and Codex.

### Related issues

- #45818 requests a shared project container/context across Chat, Work, and Codex.
- #43839 proposes branch conversations that merge back into a parent thread.
- #38260 intentionally keeps multiple chats separate while sharing selected project context.

This request is different: it is about **consolidating several already-independent conversations/tasks into one new continuing thread, while automatically archiving the source threads so the workspace becomes simpler rather than more cluttered**.

items.body: ### What variant of Codex are you using? Codex in the ChatGPT Android app, connected to Codex Desktop on a Windows PC. ### What feature would you like to see? #### Current problem The pending-task queue is permanently expanded in the conversation and cannot be collapsed. With two or more queued tasks, it already obstructs the chat. As more tasks are added, the queue occupies almost the entire available screen, making it difficult to read Codex's responses and follow the current task. Reordering is also cumbersome: moving a task from the bottom to the top requires repeatedly opening its menu and selecting “Move up”. #### Requested behavior 1. **Compact queue control** Replace the permanently expanded list with a compact “Queue · N” button so the conversation remains readable regardless of the queue length. 2. **Dedicated queue manager** Tapping the button should open a modal or bottom sheet containing the pending tasks. The list should scroll independently. Closing the modal should restore the previous conversation scroll position. 3. **Drag-and-drop reordering** Give each task a touch-friendly drag handle on the left. Users should be able to drag a task directly to any position in one gesture, with clear feedback showing the drop position. Keep the resulting execution order synchronized with Codex Desktop. 4. **Task actions** Place a vertical three-dot button on the right of each task. Its menu should contain: - “Edit message”: view and edit the full queued prompt. - “Steer instead”: send the instruction to the current turn instead of leaving it queued. - “Cancel message”: remove the task from the queue. Remove “Move up” and “Move down” from this menu. Reordering should use the dedicated drag handle. 5. **Add new tasks** Include an “Add a task…” input inside the queue manager so users can add pending tasks without closing it. Please keep the design consistent with the existing ChatGPT/Codex interface and avoid adding unnecessary controls. The attached mockups illustrate the proposed interaction. This would make it much easier to monitor ongoing work and organize follow-up tasks from a phone. ### Additional information #### Environment - ChatGPT Android app: 1.2026.265 - Android: 16, build BP2A.250605.031.A3 - HyperOS: 3.0.302.0 - Desktop host: Codex Desktop - Host OS: Windows 11 Pro, version 25H2, OS build 26200.9457 #### Steps to observe the current behavior 1. Try moving the last task to the first position using the repeated “Move up” action. #### Current interface The screenshot below shows the current expanded queue. Collapsed queue in the conversation** **2. Open queue manager** **3. Drag-and-drop reordering** **4. Task-actions menu**

When I returned, the same request appeared in two conversations. The additional Work conversation displayed **GPT-6 Astra / Ultra / Custom permissions** and had completed its answer. The original Pro conversation remained stuck with **“Connection interrupted. Waiting for the complete answer.”** It eventually displayed the completed answer, and its title changed as well.

The main issue is the unexplained system-created Work conversation and its different model setting. The delayed result display is an additional symptom, not an explanation for the model/execution-mode change.

## Environment

- Windows 11 25H2, 64-bit, build 26200.9168
- App package version: 26.930.7945.0

## Steps observed

1. Select 6 Pro in Chat.
2. Submit one request for a comprehensive, source-backed web research report.
3. Leave the computer without further interaction.
4. Return to find both the original Chat and a separate Work conversation containing the same request.
5. Observe Astra Ultra and Custom permissions in the Work conversation, while the original Chat still displays the connection-interrupted message.
6. The original Chat eventually displays the completed result.

This is an observed occurrence, not a claim that these steps reproduce the problem every time.

## Timeline

All events below occurred on October 6, 2026. JST is UTC+09:00.

- Original Chat recorded creation: 20:46:51.000778 JST / 11:46:51.000778 UTC
- Work recorded creation: 20:46:59 JST / 11:46:59 UTC, approximately eight seconds later. The Work timestamp has only second-level precision
- Work completion notification recorded locally: 21:31:25 JST / 12:31:25 UTC
- Original Chat stream error: 21:32:30 JST / 12:32:30 UTC, “404 / Resume stream unavailable”
- Stream recovery succeeded: 21:46:01 JST / 12:46:01 UTC, attempt=72
- Around 21:46 JST, I observed the original Chat finally display the completed answer and a changed title

A value presented as completedAt at 21:24:27 JST was found to be derived from the final message's creation timestamp. It must not be treated as verified execution completion time.

## Verified observations

- The request text matched exactly, and both conversations referenced the same three output artifacts
- Progress text in the original Chat matched the Work conversation's recorded progress
- I normally use Full access for manually created Work conversations. I did not select Custom
- Two known assistant-created Work conversations also resolve to Custom under the app's permission-display logic. The affected Work conversation likewise resolves to Custom, although the underlying permission configurations differ
- Chat mode itself does not have the Work access-permission selector. The permission comparison concerns Work conversations only; assistant-created automations must not be classified as manually created conversations

Together with my absence and lack of interaction, these observations support that the additional Work conversation was generated by the system.

## Expected behavior

A request submitted with 6 Pro should honor that selection. If the product delegates work or creates another execution conversation, it should clearly explain that relationship and which model actually runs the task. It should not leave two conversations with unexplained model and permission displays.

## What remains unknown

The actual inference model has not been verified. Astra Ultra is the observed setting in the Work UI; I am not claiming that this display alone proves which model generated the answer.

The available read-only investigation did not establish the exact creation trigger or model assignment.

Please investigate:

1. Why a Chat request submitted with 6 Pro generated a separate Work conversation without a user handoff action
2. Whether this was delegation, conversion, synchronization, or an unintended duplicate execution
3. How the requested Chat model, the Work model setting, and the actual inference model relate in this case
4. Why the generated Work conversation used Custom permissions despite the saved Full access defaults
5. Why the original Chat could not resume its response stream after the Work result was available
6. Why the original conversation title changed during this sequence

The relevant creation window is October 6, 2026, 11:46:40–11:47:08 UTC. The result-delivery and recovery window is 12:31–12:46 UTC.

The available tools in this session did not expose a dedicated ChatGPT chat-management bulk operation. The agent therefore performed repeated browser clicks, confirmations, and list checks. This workflow was slow enough that the user stopped it and chose to delete the chats manually.

- The agent workflow added repeated per-item page reads and verification round trips.
- Deletion dialogs and row removal did not always update together. A dialog could close while the old row remained in a subsequent snapshot; pending deletion also disabled controls.
- Calls waiting for the deletion dialog to become hidden returned selector deadline errors after roughly 3 seconds even when a longer timeout was requested. Please investigate whether the browser bridge imposes a shorter deadline and how pending operations should be represented.

items.body:
### Environment

- ChatGPT / Codex unified desktop experience
- Project-based Chat workflow
- Observed on Windows

### Summary

When I use **Pin** on a chat that already belongs to a Project, the pin action promotes that chat to the **global/top-level pinned area outside the Project**.

From a project-scoped workflow, this is surprising. The action is invoked while the chat is inside a Project, so the natural expectation is that the chat remains inside that Project and is promoted only to the top of that Project's chat list.

### Reproduction

1. Open a ChatGPT Project containing multiple chats.
2. Select one chat inside that Project.
3. Choose **Pin** for that chat.
4. Observe where the chat appears in the sidebar.

### Actual behavior

The pinned chat is promoted out of the Project's local ordering and appears in the global pinned/top-level area.

This weakens the Project as an organizational boundary: pinning an important project chat effectively pulls its navigation entry outside the workspace where it belongs.

### Expected behavior

When **Pin** is invoked on a chat that belongs to a Project:

- the chat should remain associated visually with that Project;
- it should move to the top of that Project's chat/session list; and
- it should remain there as a project-local pinned item.

If both behaviors are desired, the UI could distinguish them explicitly, for example:

- **Pin in project**
- **Pin globally**

But a project-local action should not silently change the chat's navigation scope.

### Why this matters

Projects are most useful when they provide a stable boundary for related Chat and Work sessions.

A user may have many Projects and many chats. The purpose of pinning a chat inside one Project is usually to make that chat easier to reach **within that Project**, not to create another item in the global sidebar.

When project chats are promoted globally, the global area becomes cluttered while the Project itself becomes less useful as the user's persistent workspace.

I would like to keep using Projects as the primary organizational unit. Pinning should strengthen that structure rather than bypass it.

### Related issues

- #39233 concerns pin eligibility/re-pinning of Project chats, not where a successfully pinned Project chat is placed.
- #48910 / #26762 discuss ordering and pinning within projects, but this report specifically concerns **pin scope: project-local vs global**.

### Environment

- ChatGPT / Codex unified desktop app on Windows
- ChatGPT Pro
- Observed on October 6, 2026
- The app recently showed version `26.930.41038` (released October 4, 2026)

### Summary

Newly created **Work** sessions no longer expose the normal **Move to project** action, even though the same Work session can still be moved into an existing Project by dragging it onto the Project in the sidebar.

Older Work sessions still retain project-move behavior, and Work created from inside a Project is correctly associated with that Project.

This makes the current behavior look like a recent UI regression or an inconsistent eligibility check rather than an intentional removal of project movement.

### Reproduction

1. Create a new Work session outside any Project.
2. Open the Work session's menu.
3. Observe that **Move to project** is unavailable.
4. In the sidebar, drag that same Work session onto an existing Project.
5. Observe that the Work session is successfully moved into the Project.
6. Compare with an older Work session created before the recent UI change; project movement remains available there.
7. Also compare with a Work session created from inside a Project; it is correctly project-scoped.

### Actual behavior

| Case | Move to project menu | Drag into Project |
|---|---|---|
| Older Work | Available / still movable | Works |
| Newly created Work outside Project | Missing | Works |
| Work created inside Project | Already scoped | N/A |

The important inconsistency is that a newly created Work session is accepted by the Project when dragged, while the explicit menu action for the same operation is missing.

### Expected behavior

For any Work session that is eligible to be moved into a Project:

- **Move to project** should remain available in the menu; and
- drag-and-drop should provide the same result as an optional convenience path.

If moving newly created Work sessions into Projects is intentionally unsupported, drag-and-drop should not silently allow the same operation. The two entry points should agree.

### User impact

This is more than a cosmetic menu issue for project-based workflows.

When the explicit move action disappears, users can reasonably conclude that Work can no longer be added to Projects. They may then:

- create replacement Work sessions unnecessarily;
- manually transfer context and instructions;
- spend significant time rebuilding an existing workflow;
- lose confidence that Projects can remain the stable home for long-running work.

I discovered the drag-and-drop workaround only by trying it intuitively after the menu option disappeared. It was not obvious that the underlying move operation still worked.

I would like to keep using **Projects as the persistent workspace**, with Chat and Work sessions organized under them. Please restore a consistent project-move UI for eligible Work sessions.

### Related

- #34300 concerns a different Chat/Work-to-Project inconsistency. This report specifically concerns **new Work sessions where the menu path is missing while drag-and-drop on the same object still succeeds**.

### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.930.61225

### What subscription do you have?

Pro 200

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26300.0 x64 + Linux 6.18.33.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2 x86_64 x86_64

### What issue are you seeing?

Using Codex Desktop’s WSL backend, Windows executables behave differently inside agent tool calls than in my normal WSL terminal.

**Environment**

- Codex Desktop app version: 26.930.61225
- WSL distribution: Ubuntu
- Windows mise: `2026.10.3 windows-x64`
- Windows uv: `0.12.23`
- mise uses native `.exe` shims.

**Observed behavior**

In my normal WSL terminal, `PATHEXT` is unset and:

```text
WSLENV=WT_SESSION:WT_PROFILE_ID:
```

The Windows `uv.exe` shim works.

Inside Codex’s WSL tool shell, `PATHEXT` is also unset, but `WSLENV` includes `PATHEXT/l`. Running the same shim fails:

```text
mise ERROR No executable found for configured tool: uv
The installed version does not provide this executable with its current backend metadata.
Reinstall it with:
mise install --force uv@0.12.23
```

The actual installed `uv.exe` works when invoked directly. Explicitly requesting `mise x -- uv.exe --version` also works.

**Controlled reproduction**

In the affected Codex WSL shell, this fails:

```bash
/mnt/d/mise/shims/uv.exe --version
```

Removing only the `PATHEXT` forwarding entry for the child process makes it succeed:

```python
import os
import subprocess

env = os.environ.copy()
env["WSLENV"] = ":".join(
    entry
    for entry in env.get("WSLENV", "").split(":")
    if entry.split("/", 1)[0].upper() != "PATHEXT"
)

subprocess.run(
    ["/mnt/d/mise/shims/uv.exe", "--version"],
    env=env,
    check=True,
)
```

No reinstallation or persistent Windows environment change is needed.

**Local investigation**

The installed Desktop JavaScript declares:

```js
{name: `PATHEXT`, type: `list`}
```

Its WSL environment builder converts this to `PATHEXT/l` and adds it without checking whether the variable has a value.

I have not established where the `PATHEXT` value disappears. The confirmed trigger is forwarding an unset value back into Windows.

**Expected behavior**

Windows programs launched from Codex’s WSL tool shells should retain working executable-extension lookup. Desktop should avoid leaving a `PATHEXT` forwarding entry that overrides Windows’ valid environment with an absent value.

Related: #15174 describes broken `PATHEXT` in Windows shell children, although its exact cause may differ.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Install mise-en-place in Windows and `mise use -g uv`.
2. Set Codex to start in WSL.
3. Ask Codex to run `uv.exe --version`.

### What is the expected behavior?

Codex sees Windows `uv`'s help.

items.title: Keep Guardian v2 WebSocket pools warm with concurrent replenishment
items.body:
Keep Guardian v2 WebSocket pools warm with concurrent replenishment

## Why

Serial connection opens let a stalled handshake delay healthy sockets. Waiting until the idle pool is empty to refill also leaves classification bursts using HTTP fallback.

## What changed

- Open up to four WebSockets concurrently and start replenishing when the idle pool falls to half capacity. Preserve successful in-flight opens when another open fails or times out.
- Make explicit prewarming wait for an existing refill before checking readiness.
- Add `ResponsesWebsocketClient::connect_with_connector` and reuse one connector per sampler, initializing TLS configuration on a blocking task while retaining per-connection authentication and destination policy checks.
- Record connection lease durations for admission, setup, and total time, tagged by transport.

## Testing

Add regression tests for a stalled handshake alongside a healthy socket and replenishment before the last idle socket is leased. Update cooldown, authentication, and transport retry tests to account for concurrent handshake completion.

### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.930.61225 (build 13232; verified from installed app bundle metadata)

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Pro (user-confirmed)

### What platform is your computer?

macOS — `uname -mprs`: `Darwin 27.0.0 arm64 arm`

### What issue are you seeing?

Observed on 2026-10-06 in the ChatGPT desktop app on macOS. Subagent model and reasoning-effort visibility differs depending on how the parent task was created.

In a manually created local chat, the main UI shows GPT-6.1 Sol / High. An Astra subagent requested with Medium effort displays GPT-6 Astra · Medium in the child panel. The user also verified Luna / Medium.

In a directly assistant-created task executing on the same Mac, the parent was requested as gpt-6.1-sol/high and the native child was explicitly requested as gpt-6-astra/medium. The child completes its task, but its panel shows only the task name Astra medium probe, without a model or effort label. The creation receipt exposes only the task name, so the parent cannot confirm the effective child configuration.

Impact: users cannot reliably audit heterogeneous model delegation or evaluate cost/quality routing.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Manually create a local chat in the desktop app and select GPT-6.1 Sol / High.
2. Request a native Astra subagent with Medium reasoning effort and inspect its panel. Observe GPT-6 Astra · Medium. Luna / Medium was also verified in a manually created local chat.
3. Ask the assistant to directly create a new task executing on the same Mac, requesting gpt-6.1-sol/high for its parent.
4. In that task, call the native spawn_agent with these explicit parameters:

```json
{
  "task_name": "astra_medium_probe",
  "model": "gpt-6-astra",
  "reasoning_effort": "medium",
  "fork_turns": "none",
  "message": "Acknowledge receipt, compute 17+25, then finish. Do not use tools or create more agents."
}
```

5. Confirm that the child acknowledges the task and returns 17+25=42.
6. Inspect the child panel: only Astra medium probe is shown, with no model or reasoning-effort label. The creation receipt contains only:

```json
{"task_name":"/root/astra_medium_probe"}
```

The requested parent configuration was not independently observable in the assistant-created task; it is a request parameter, not evidence of the effective serving model.

### What is the expected behavior?

Model and reasoning configuration should be consistently visible in active/completed subagent panels and/or exposed through supported task metadata, regardless of how the parent task was created. For this requested child, the panel should show the effective model and effort, such as GPT-6 Astra · Medium, or explicitly explain any inherited/fallback configuration.

### Additional information

Public task metadata showed local for one user-created example and durable for an assistant-created example. This is a correlation only; it is not an established cause.

This report concerns display and observability. It does not claim the model override was ignored or identify a backend root cause.

Related reports: #32283 and #32125 describe missing subagent UI details; #32504 concerns effective metadata in canonical activity items. This report adds a same-Mac comparison between manually created local chats and directly assistant-created tasks.

App version was verified from the installed app's standard bundle metadata; subscription was confirmed by the user. Redacted comparison screenshots can be provided if needed. No private session IDs, project contents, local paths, logs, or screenshots are included.

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

ChatGPT/Codex desktop on Windows, with a dot coordinating work on an authorized connected Windows computer. Current installed MSIX: `OpenAI.Codex 26.930.7945.0` (package metadata; About-dialog display version unverified). Windows NT `10.0.22631.0` x64. The standalone CLI was used only to submit text feedback.

### What feature would you like to see?

Please add **capability-aware task routing, supported recovery, and verified completion for dots**, so that authorized tasks on a connected computer can be completed reliably with fewer manual interventions.

A connected/authorized indicator does not tell the user whether the specific delegated task can actually use their browser, native Windows apps, or local files. A dot should check these concrete capabilities before choosing an execution route or promising to do the work.

Requested behavior and acceptance criteria:

1. **Check capabilities before delegation.** Validate the selected computer, execution environment, required tool readiness and applicable permissions. Distinguish personal Chrome, the in-app browser, the cloud browser, native Windows Computer Use, and shell/file access. Show which of these are usable for the particular task. If a capability is intentionally unsupported, say so and identify a supported route.

2. **Recover from transient failures through supported mechanisms.** Provide bounded retry/backoff and a clear Retry action for tool startup and capture failures. Expose an actionable reason when recovery fails, instead of only "MCP server failed to start." Do not repeatedly send the same failing task back to the user.

3. **Try appropriate, authorized alternatives before asking for manual work.** For example, if public/cloud retrieval of a requested page fails and connected-browser access is available and allowed, check that route before asking the user to upload a screenshot. Do not switch routes to evade explicit policy denials, access controls, or a missing required authorization.

4. **Verify the actual result before reporting completion.** A worker turn ending or a tool call being accepted should not alone count as success. Check the requested deliverable, the exact file/version and save state, or the remote end state where applicable. Make incomplete work and remaining user actions explicit.

5. **Preserve context and ownership across delegation.** Carry the necessary task context and scoped user authorization through the supported delegation mechanism. Retain responsibility for the requested outcome and follow-up after a worker returns an error or partial result.

6. **Make capability differences visible and documented.** Explain the supported differences between ordinary local chats, dot-created tasks on the same computer, and cloud work. Installed skills or enabled plugins should not be presented as proof that their initialization tools are exposed to a particular worker.

These requirements should be validated with end-to-end Windows tests covering successful tasks, intermittent capture/tool failures, unavailable capabilities and appropriate authorization blockers.

### Additional information

This enhancement request follows an authorized read-only review of existing October 6, 2026 task histories and local desktop logs. The observations below are distinct symptoms; no common root cause is asserted:

- Appshot attempts failed with `computer-use request timed out: load_appshot_capture_source` and `failureReason=native_completion_failed`, with successful captures interleaved. The exact failing-app attribution and the timeout's underlying cause remain unknown.
- The hosted dot's main thread logged failures for `cua_repl` and `codex_apps`. Later delegated calls successfully navigated an existing signed-in Chrome session, so browser access was not universally broken.
- One delegated PC task reported that its native Windows Computer Use JavaScript route was not exposed, while local file/cache reads worked. A separate ordinary local chat successfully imported the documented `@oai/sky` package and called `sky.list_windows()`. This confirms native window inventory in that local chat, not screenshot/control parity or a full same-build comparison.
- For one requested public X-post analysis, the retained task performed public web retrieval/search and then asked the user for a screenshot. No connected-browser attempt was present. Whether that alternative would have succeeded is untested.

An earlier same-day delegated-task report verified desktop MSIX `26.930.4958.0`; the current package check found `26.930.7945.0`. The logged capture failures preceded the current package check. No complete post-update reproduction or confirmed repair is claimed.

Related existing reports, reviewed to avoid opening duplicate bug reports:

- #45353 — Windows Appshot source-loading timeout.
- #51328 and #49458 — native desktop capabilities missing from dot-delegated tasks.
- #49562 — Windows delegated-tool startup/path diagnostics.
- #49883 — incomplete delegated-work follow-through.
- #50544 — local-executor recovery and persistent local workflows.

This request focuses on a user-visible reliability contract for routing, recovery and outcome verification across those workflows. Please consolidate or route it to the responsible product team if an existing tracking issue already covers that scope.

Direct OpenAI feedback was submitted first. The CLI confirmed **"Feedback recorded (no logs)"** with receipt/thread ID:
`01a1119f-6f6e-7010-8e41-1027a5642070`

Feedback reference only: the CLI's autogenerated link selected its CLI template because it was the transport. The affected product and this request concern the Windows desktop/dots workflow.

Official behavior references:
- https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/dots/computers-and-apps
- https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/dots/tasks-and-memory

Only sanitized technical observations are included. No raw logs, screenshots, private conversation contents, local user paths, account identifiers or personal documents are attached.

labels.name: enhancement

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

Codex Desktop App (Windows)

### What feature would you like to see?

#### Explore every question without losing the thread.

I believe passage-anchored follow-ups could transform how we learn complex topics through AI conversations, keeping the main explanation coherent while making deeper questions easy to revisit.

Let users select a term or passage in an assistant response and open a **persistent, multi-turn annotation conversation attached to that exact passage**, similar to comments in a document editor.

The main conversation would keep its reading order, while detailed follow-ups remain discoverable where the questions arose.

This interaction pattern could benefit **ChatGPT, Work, and Codex** wherever users need to explore details without interrupting a longer conversation. This issue requests consideration for Codex Desktop; the broader applicability is part of the product idea, not a claim that these products already support it.

#### Problem and motivation

When I use an assistant to understand a complex topic, I need a coherent main explanation and room to investigate individual details. For example, a Transformer lesson might progress through Q/K/V, attention weights, and multi-head attention. Questions about one projection matrix or one formula can take several turns.

Appending every clarification to the main chat makes the explanation difficult to reread. Moving them to separate chats makes their connection to the original passage harder to find.

This also applies to Codex workflows: understanding an unfamiliar codebase, reviewing an architectural explanation, or asking about a particular step in a plan without interrupting the main task. The learning example below illustrates the interaction rather than requiring a dedicated education mode.

#### Proposed interaction

1. Select text in an assistant response and choose **Ask in annotation**.
2. Open a side panel containing the source quote and a separate follow-up conversation. Allow multiple turns in that annotation.
3. Keep a visible indicator on the original passage. Hover or keyboard focus previews the follow-up; clicking reopens it. Tapping should provide an equivalent interaction.
4. Preserve the annotation and its source relationship when the conversation is reopened.
5. Optionally allow selecting text in an annotation answer to create a child annotation.
6. Provide a collapsible review tree of recorded follow-ups, with links back to their source passages.
7. Let users explicitly bring a useful branch conclusion into the main conversation.

#### Availability without added clutter

The feature should be **available by default, appear on demand, and be fully disableable in settings**. Ordinary chats should retain their familiar layout. Selecting text would reveal an “Ask in annotation” action; the annotation panel would open only when the user chooses it. Indicators would appear only on passages that have annotations, and the review tree would be relevant only once annotations exist. Closing the panel would return to the regular chat layout. A user who prefers a simpler experience could turn the feature off entirely.

This separates feature availability from panel visibility, so short questions do not require an annotation mode or a permanently visible sidebar.

**Example:**

```text
Main explanation: Q/K/V → attention weights → multi-head attention
  ├─ “separate learned projection matrices”
  │   └─ Why do Q and K use different matrices?
  │       └─ “Matching relationships do not have to be symmetric”
  │           └─ What does “not symmetric” mean here?
  └─ “divides by √dₖ”
      └─ Why divide by the square root of the dimension?
```

The questions stay attached to their source, while the main explanation can be read continuously.

#### Suggested first version

The core request is **text selection + a persistent annotation panel + reopening from the source passage**. A flat annotation list would be sufficient initially. Nested annotations, the review tree, and bringing conclusions back could follow later.

The tree would show actual conversation relationships. It does not need to infer a knowledge graph.

#### Context and anchor behavior

- An annotation should receive the selected passage, relevant context up to that point, and its own history. Unrelated branches should not be included by default.
- Branch messages should not silently enter the main transcript or steer an active main task. Bringing a conclusion back should be explicit.
- Anchors should identify the source message and answer version. If a response is edited or regenerated, retain the original association or show that reassociation is needed; do not silently attach the annotation to a different passage.
- Source quotes, follow-up history, and parent/child relationships should survive closing and reopening the conversation.

These are desired product behaviors, not claims that the prototype implements production context management or answer-version handling.


### Additional information

#### Interaction prototype

I built an independent, dark-theme English prototype to make the interaction concrete. It demonstrates passage selection, hover previews, multi-turn annotations, nested follow-ups, a review tree, local persistence, and Markdown note export.

**All assistant responses are predefined examples.** It does not call a model, connect to the official Codex desktop app, or read existing Codex chats. It is a demonstration of the proposed interaction, not an implementation intended for merging into Codex.

The demo is a self-contained HTML file. To try the accompanying ZIP, extract it and open `CodexAnnotation-demo.html` in a modern desktop browser. No installation, account, API key, or server is required. Local saving depends on browser permissions; exported notes provide a separate way to keep a session.

Suggested walkthrough: select a passage → ask in an annotation → continue the follow-up → select part of the answer to create a child annotation → open the tree → jump back to the source.

#### Video walkthrough

A short recording showing passage-linked annotations, hover previews, nested follow-ups, and explicitly bringing an answer back to the main conversation. This is the independent prototype with predefined example responses.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/7a0b6175-bb3b-4c3d-8007-51f8cdd558be

#### Related requests and distinct scope

- [#26227 — Persist side chats as child threads attached to the main thread](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/26227): closely related persistence and parent/child organization. This request adds a visible anchor to a **specific selected passage** within an answer.
- [#12450 — Support for Tree-based Conversation Management](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/12450): related branching and tree navigation. Here, the emphasis is passage-local clarification and continuous rereading of the main explanation.
- [#26198 — Selection-based comments in Markdown and HTML previews](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/26198): related selection and source context. This request concerns assistant chat responses and keeps each follow-up transcript separate from the main conversation.

I am opening this separately to make the passage-anchored interaction and prototype easy to evaluate. If the maintainers consider it part of an existing request, I would be happy for it to be consolidated there.

Would this interaction fit Codex Desktop? Feedback on the smallest useful scope, or guidance on routing the broader learning use case to the ChatGPT team, would be welcome.


#### Demo screenshots

**Passage-attached follow-up and a nested annotation:**

![Passage-attached annotation in the independent prototype](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/641948fe-441d-4630-8731-dc866e6fb403)

**Review tree organized by source passage:**

![Nested follow-up tree in the independent prototype](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/7a4a7388-f806-4e18-a518-def0fec9faa6)

#### Download the interaction demo

[CodexAnnotation-demo.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33110175/CodexAnnotation-demo.zip)

I’d be happy to discuss the interaction design or provide additional prototype details. Please feel free to reach out here on GitHub.
