items.title: Voice with a custom model provider sends the provider's env_key credential to chatgpt.com (401 "Could not parse your authentication token")

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: auth
labels.description: Issues related to authentication and accounts

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: custom-model
labels.description: Issues related to custom model providers (including local models)

items.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?

TUI: `codex-cli 0.158.0`. The shared app-server daemon had auto-updated to `0.160.0`. The functions cited below are unchanged between `rust-v0.158.0` and `rust-v0.160.0`; links point at `rust-v0.160.0` (a956835d).

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Plus, signed in with ChatGPT.

### Which model were you using?

`gpt-6-astra` through a custom model provider (a local OpenAI-compatible gateway).

### What platform is your computer?

`Linux 7.2.8-1-cachyos x86_64 unknown`

### What terminal emulator and version are you using (if applicable)?

Ghostty 1.3.1

### What issue are you seeing?

I'm signed in with ChatGPT, and model requests go through a custom provider that has its own key. Starting voice fails with:

```
unexpected status 401 Unauthorized: {"detail":"Could not parse your authentication token. Please try signing in again."}, url: https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/realtime/calls?intent=quicksilver&architecture=avas, cf-ray: a45e3a335b661203-MAA, request id: 68dbc8ab-727a-4275-a4fb-510326b45d33
```

Config:

```toml
model_provider = "my_gateway"
experimental_realtime_webrtc_call_base_url = "https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex"

[model_providers.my_gateway]
name = "OpenAI"
base_url = "http://localhost:4141"
env_key = "MY_GATEWAY_API_KEY"
requires_openai_auth = true
wire_api = "responses"
```

The override is there because otherwise call creation goes to the gateway (`http://localhost:4141/live` for the V3 path the TUI uses), and the gateway doesn't implement realtime ([realtime_call.rs#L72](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/a956835d020762cb2b570053af06f643a11c0ecc/codex-rs/codex-api/src/endpoint/realtime_call.rs#L72)).

With this config, the experimental WebRTC call URL override keeps the custom provider's resolved credentials and headers:

1. `/voice` starts a WebRTC, realtime V3 session ([app_server_session/realtime.rs#L50-L51](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/a956835d020762cb2b570053af06f643a11c0ecc/codex-rs/tui/src/app_server_session/realtime.rs#L50-L51)).
2. `experimental_realtime_webrtc_call_base_url` replaces `base_url` on a copy of the configured provider; credentials are resolved separately ([realtime_conversation.rs#L1354-L1361](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/a956835d020762cb2b570053af06f643a11c0ecc/codex-rs/core/src/realtime_conversation.rs#L1354-L1361)).
3. `create_realtime_call_with_headers` authenticates with the configured provider's `api_auth`, and copies the same auth into the sideband WebSocket headers ([client.rs#L669-L703](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/a956835d020762cb2b570053af06f643a11c0ecc/codex-rs/core/src/client.rs#L669-L703)).
4. For a provider with `env_key`, `resolve_provider_auth` returns `Bearer $env_key` before it considers `requires_openai_auth` or the ChatGPT session ([auth.rs#L197-L222](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/a956835d020762cb2b570053af06f643a11c0ecc/codex-rs/model-provider/src/auth.rs#L197-L222), [auth.rs#L292-L304](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/a956835d020762cb2b570053af06f643a11c0ecc/codex-rs/model-provider/src/auth.rs#L292-L304)).

So `Authorization: Bearer $MY_GATEWAY_API_KEY` goes to `chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/realtime/calls`. If call creation succeeded, the same header would go to the sideband, which defaults to `api.openai.com/v1` when `experimental_realtime_ws_base_url` is unset ([methods.rs#L62](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/a956835d020762cb2b570053af06f643a11c0ecc/codex-rs/codex-api/src/endpoint/realtime_websocket/methods.rs#L62), [methods.rs#L849](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/a956835d020762cb2b570053af06f643a11c0ecc/codex-rs/codex-api/src/endpoint/realtime_websocket/methods.rs#L849)).

I realise the override is documented as "Experimental / do not use. Overrides only the WebRTC realtime call creation base URL" ([config_toml.rs#L436-L439](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/a956835d020762cb2b570053af06f643a11c0ecc/codex-rs/config/src/config_toml.rs#L436-L439)), so for the URL this may be working as designed. The issues are:

- There's no supported way to use voice with ChatGPT auth while model requests go through a custom provider with its own credential. `[realtime]` only has `version`, `type`, `transport` and `voice` ([config_toml.rs#L655](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/a956835d020762cb2b570053af06f643a11c0ecc/codex-rs/config/src/config_toml.rs#L655)).
- The custom provider's credential ends up at OpenAI hosts: chatgpt.com via the call override, and api.openai.com via the built-in sideband default.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Sign in with ChatGPT (`codex login`).
2. Use the config above with any OpenAI-compatible gateway as `base_url`.
3. Make sure `MY_GATEWAY_API_KEY` is set in the app-server's environment (e.g. export it, then `codex app-server daemon restart`).
4. Start the TUI, start a conversation, then run `/voice`.
5. Call creation returns 401 "Could not parse your authentication token" from chatgpt.com.

### What is the expected behavior?

Provide a way to use ChatGPT authentication for WebRTC call creation and its sideband, while keeping custom-provider authentication for model requests. For example, a `[realtime]` setting that selects a different provider than `model_provider`, or using the signed-in ChatGPT auth when the realtime URLs point at OpenAI hosts.

Separately, it would be safer not to send a provider's `env_key` / `experimental_bearer_token` credential to a host other than that provider's `base_url`.

### Additional information

Possible workaround for ordinary ChatGPT-authenticated sessions (worked out from the source; I haven't tested it end to end yet), if the gateway accepts its key in a header other than `Authorization`: replace `env_key` with `env_http_headers = { "x-api-key" = "MY_GATEWAY_API_KEY" }` and keep `requires_openai_auth = true`. The provider then takes the first-party auth path, so call creation and the sideband get the ChatGPT bearer token. This only separates header names, not destinations: the gateway key still goes to OpenAI as `x-api-key` (provider headers are merged into realtime requests), and the ChatGPT token goes to the gateway on model requests.

Happy to provide `codex doctor --json` output if useful.

items.title: [Feature] Support negotiated Org/Portable Org output formats

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

items.body:
## Problem

Codex clients can consume machine-readable results, but there is no negotiated content format for clients that want to render agent replies natively as Emacs Org-mode. Prompting the model to emit Org syntax is unreliable across streaming chunks, tool results, and replay, and a JSON envelope does not describe the markup language of each text block.

## Proposed solution

Add an optional interoperable `text/org` format with a `portable` profile to Codex output and ACP-facing integrations.

- Keep all existing text and JSON behavior unchanged.
- Let clients advertise accepted formats and negotiate `text/org` when supported.
- Carry the selected format/profile with each text content block and preserve it across streaming events and replay.
- Fall back to Markdown or plain text when the agent or client does not support Org.

Please coordinate the wire-level design with the ACP RFD: https://github.com/agentclientprotocol/agent-client-protocol/pull/2315.

## Use case

An ACP client running in Emacs can render headlines, paragraphs, lists, links, tables, and safe static blocks as native Org-mode while the response is streaming. This provides a stable contract for agents and clients instead of a prompt-only convention.

Related output-format discussion: https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/16733

### What issue are you seeing?

Codex discovers Chrome as an extension-backed browser, but cannot enumerate its tabs or create a new tab. Browser operations fail after approximately 21–22 seconds with:

```text
nodeRepl.fetch request failed
```

This blocks a simple user request to open a public website in Chrome.

The initial `await cua.getState()` returned Chrome provider metadata, then an inventory error:

```json
{

      "tabs": []
    }
  ],

  ]
}
```

Chrome profile name and extension/session identifiers have been omitted. The empty tab array is returned alongside an error, so it does not establish that Chrome actually had no tabs. The other browser providers were listed; their navigation functionality was not tested.

Relevant redacted stack frames from the initial failure:

```text
Error: nodeRepl.fetch request failed
    at <TEMP>\kernel.js:1595:16
    at Object.settle (<TEMP>\worker-runtime.js:396:5)
    at <TEMP>\kernel.js:1871:11
    at handleInputFrame (<TEMP>\worker-runtime.js:418:7)
    at Socket.<anonymous> (<TEMP>\worker-runtime.js:434:9)
```

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. In the Windows Codex desktop app, ask the agent to test the Chrome connection.
2. Call `await cua.getState()`. Chrome appears in the inventory as an extension-backed provider, but tab enumeration fails with the error above. The observed tool duration was 21.789 seconds.
3. Explicitly mention `@Chrome` using `plugin://browser@openai-bundled?browserFamily=chrome` and ask it to open Baidu (`https://www.baidu.com`).
4. Refresh browser discovery using `await cua.listBrowsers()`. This succeeds and reports Chrome with current provider ID `"4"` and the same extension instance as before.
5. Use the newly discovered ID to create a tab:

```javascript
await cua.createBrowserTab("4", "https://www.baidu.com");
```

6. This fails again with `nodeRepl.fetch request failed` after 21.326 seconds. No successful tab creation or page load was confirmed.

The IDs above are observed session values, not stable IDs to reuse in another session. Use the current Chrome ID from discovery when reproducing.

### What is the expected behavior?

When the connected Chrome extension is discovered, Codex should be able to enumerate its tabs and open a new tab at `https://www.baidu.com`.

If the extension transport is unavailable, the error should identify the failure and provide a supported recovery step instead of only exposing a generic fetch failure.

### Additional information

Two separate intermediate errors occurred before the final attempt:
- Reusing the previous provider ID `"3"` returned `Browser is not available: 3`; discovery then returned ID `"4"`.
- Passing `{ visible: true }` to `createBrowserTab` returned `Capability is not available: visibility`. Removing that option and using the current provider ID still produced the fetch failure above.

These intermediate errors were corrected before the final failed tab request. Their relationship to the transport failure is unknown.

Related reports: #44383, #46095, #50837, and #50675 (Edge).

This report adds the exact current Windows app/Chrome versions, successful provider discovery, and a failed tab-creation attempt using the freshly discovered provider ID. No proxy/TLS/root-cause conclusion is established by the evidence collected here.

A consumer that treats SessionEnd as "the agent in this terminal exited" tears down the live conversation's state.

Log (session truncated):
+0s   SessionEnd        session=01a11105-3861 reason=other   ← replaced startup session, 60s after /resume
...
      SessionStart      source=resume session=01a110e4-52e2  ← only with the first prompt
      UserPromptSubmit  session=01a110e4-52e2

Ask: fire SessionStart (source: "resume") when /resume selects a conversation, and either pair the startup session's SessionEnd with a SessionStart or skip it for a session that never started a turn.

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

Codex App. The tool integration could also benefit the CLI and IDE extension, with inline rendering available on supported graphical surfaces. The same score-artifact approach would also be useful in ChatGPT conversations.

### What feature would you like to see?

I would like Codex to support musical scores as structured, interactive artifacts inside the conversation.

Users should be able to request a musical example, import an existing score, or transcribe an image, then see actual staff notation and guitar/bass tablature directly in chat. The same artifact should support playback, conversational revisions, and export.

This would be useful for music education, instrument practice, composition, arranging, transcription, and development of music software.

#### Expected user experience

Examples of requests:

- “Write an eight-bar guitar exercise and show both notation and tablature.”
- “Open this MusicXML file, display the guitar part, and play it.”
- “Render this LilyPond or ABC notation text directly in the conversation.”
- “Transpose this melody down a whole step.”
- “Change measures 3–4 while preserving the rest.”
- “Convert this scanned page into an editable score and highlight uncertain passages.”
- “Export this example as SVG, PNG, PDF, MusicXML, or MIDI.”

The score should appear alongside the explanation, with readable notation, zoom, and pagination where needed. An interactive version could provide play/pause, tempo adjustment, looping, track selection, and a playback cursor synchronized with the score.

Each revision should retain an editable source so the user can continue working with the same score.

#### Existing open source tools

The following projects cover complementary parts of this workflow:

| Project | Main technology | Relevant capabilities |
|---|---|---|
| [alphaTab](https://github.com/CoderLine/alphaTab) | TypeScript, with additional platform targets | Standard notation and tablature rendering, MusicXML/Guitar Pro/AlphaTex import, SVG and canvas rendering, and integrated MIDI/SoundFont playback with interactive controls. [Documentation](https://alphatab.net/docs/introduction). |
| [Verovio](https://github.com/rism-digital/verovio) | C++, with JavaScript and Python bindings among others | Music engraving into SVG, MusicXML import through conversion to its internal representation, MEI support, and MIDI export. Suitable for compact notation previews and scalable score images. |
| [MuseScore Studio](https://github.com/musescore/MuseScore) | Primarily C++ | Score editing, standard notation and tablature, playback, and import/export. Its [command-line converter](https://handbook.musescore.org/appendix/command-line-usage) supports formats including MusicXML, MIDI, SVG, PNG, and PDF. |
| [LilyPond](https://lilypond.org/) | Text-based notation compiler and CLI | Converts textual `.ly` music descriptions into engraved scores. Supports PDF, SVG, PNG, and MIDI generation. A natural fit for model-generated musical source and high-quality exports. [Text input](https://lilypond.org/text-input.html), [CLI and output formats](https://lilypond.org/doc/v2.24/Documentation/usage/command_002dline-usage). |
| [abcjs](https://github.com/paulrosen/abcjs) | JavaScript | Converts textual ABC notation into browser-rendered scores, with playback and MIDI capabilities. Useful for compact musical examples embedded in a conversation. [Documentation](https://docs.abcjs.net/). |
| [VexFlow](https://github.com/vexflow/vexflow) | TypeScript | Renders standard notation and guitar tablature through SVG or HTML Canvas. Provides programmatic notation APIs and EasyScore syntax for concise examples; format parsing and playback can be supplied by an integration layer. |
| [Audiveris](https://github.com/Audiveris/audiveris) | Java | Optical Music Recognition: transcription of printed score images into symbolic musical data and MusicXML. Includes manual correction tools and a [batch CLI](https://audiveris.github.io/audiveris/_pages/guides/advanced/cli/). |
| [Tesseract OCR](https://github.com/tesseract-ocr/tesseract) | Primarily C++, with C/C++ APIs | Recognition of textual content such as lyrics and annotations. Audiveris already uses it for text recognition; musical transcription is handled by the OMR engine. |

MusicXML is an interchange format; AlphaTex, LilyPond syntax, and ABC notation are textual ways to describe music. These would be useful inputs for model-generated scores, with each format routed to an appropriate tool.

There is also an existing community integration example: my [GuitarPro Tab Composer](https://github.com/sgabenov/gpt-plugin-guitarpro-tab-composer), an open source local plugin combining a skill, MCP tools, and an alphaTab player. Its documented scope includes structured score generation, notation/tablature rendering, playback, and Guitar Pro/AlphaTex/SVG exports. It illustrates a possible integration approach rather than establishing native support across Codex clients.

### Additional information

#### Suggested implementation approach

A stable score-artifact interface could connect Codex to interchangeable rendering, playback, transcription, and export tools.

For example:

- Structured score or MusicXML → renderer → inline notation.
- Guitar score with tuning and fingering information → alphaTab → notation, tablature, and playback.
- LilyPond source → LilyPond CLI → SVG/PNG preview and PDF export, with MIDI when requested.
- ABC notation text → abcjs → inline notation and playback.
- Programmatic notation data or EasyScore → VexFlow → SVG/canvas preview.
- Printed score image or scanned PDF → Audiveris → MusicXML → validation and rendering.
- Editable score → export adapter → supported image, document, or music formats.

The integration could be delivered through supported skills, plugins, or MCP tools, with a consistent in-chat presentation layer. Optional tools could be installed locally or supplied through managed integrations.

The projects have different licenses, including MIT, MPL, LGPL, GPL, AGPL, and Apache licenses. The packaging and integration approach should respect each component’s license. The list describes alternative or complementary tools; an initial release could select a small subset.

#### Musical correctness and format preservation

Rendered notation should come from validated musical data. Validation should cover pitches, durations, rests, meter, ties, tuplets, and instrument constraints.

Converting pitched notation into tablature requires instrument tuning and string/fret choices. A pitch can have multiple playable positions, so generated fingering should be reviewable. Existing fingering information should be preserved when supported.

OMR results should remain editable and indicate uncertainty. Audiveris currently focuses on printed standard notation; its detection of tablature does not provide tablature transcription.

Imports and exports should report unsupported features and preserve the original file. Format conversion should not silently discard musical information.

#### Future model training and evaluation

Alongside the user interface and tooling, I would like future Codex models to receive stronger training and evaluation for symbolic music workflows:

- Generating valid MusicXML, AlphaTex, LilyPond source, ABC notation, and structured score data.
- Choosing and invoking appropriate rendering, playback, OMR, and export tools.
- Editing selected measures while preserving unrelated musical content.
- Producing playable guitar/bass fingering for a specified tuning.
- Checking rhythm and notation consistency.
- Recognizing transcription uncertainty and requesting targeted corrections.
- Using rendered scores and tool diagnostics to verify the result.

Training and evaluation could use appropriately licensed examples connecting musical instructions, symbolic scores, rendered notation, and expected tool operations.

Rendering and export can be introduced using existing tools, while improvements to model training can proceed separately. If ChatGPT product feedback or model training feedback belongs outside this repository, please route those parts to the appropriate team.

#### Initial milestone

A useful first release would support MusicXML input and at least one concise textual notation format, inline staff notation, an optional tablature view where suitable data is available, playback, SVG/PNG export, and downloadable editable source.

OMR, advanced fingering generation, additional exporters, and richer score editing could follow incrementally.

items.title: Add bounded diagnostics for agent spawn failures
items.body:
Add bounded diagnostics for agent spawn failures

## Why

Spawn failures can share an error kind and message despite different causes, such as execution and residency capacity limits. Telemetry needs enough detail to distinguish these failures without using error messages or correlation IDs as metric labels.

## What changed

- Add `AgentErrorContext` annotations for capacity limits, registry rejections, runtime availability, and spawn stages. Preserve the first annotation so outer stages retain the more precise failure origin.
- Add bounded `detail` and `error_kind` labels to spawn failure metrics, using `unknown` when no context is available.
- Emit spawn failure trace events with these classifications and the call and turn IDs for both multi-agent versions.

## Testing

Add tests for distinct capacity and registry failure contexts, preservation of manager, fork, and shutdown errors, and metric aggregation across different error messages and correlation IDs. Verify that annotations preserve existing error kinds and user-visible messages.

items.title: gpt-6.1-sol: the Codex backend rejects `prompt_cache_breakpoint`, so multi-turn requests never read from cache

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: rate-limits
labels.description: Issues related to rate limits, quotas, and token usage reporting

items.body:
### What happened

GPT-6.1 Sol's prompt caching depends on explicit breakpoints for multi-turn work: per the [prompt caching guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching), from GPT-5.6 on a request with a stable prefix and a new tail returns `cached_tokens: 0` unless a `prompt_cache_breakpoint` marks where the reusable prefix ends. But `chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex` rejects that field for gpt-6.1-sol:

```
400 invalid_request_error: "prompt_cache_breakpoint is not supported on this model"
(param: prompt_cache_breakpoint, code: invalid_parameter)
```

So on the Codex backend there is no way to get cache reads on the turns a conversation re-sends.

### Measured

2026-10-06, ChatGPT login, gpt-6.1-sol, Responses API over HTTPS with SSE, `store: false`:

- Multi-turn conversations with the earlier turns re-sent byte for byte, tool rounds included: `cached_tokens: 0` on every call.
- Adding `"prompt_cache_breakpoint": {"mode": "explicit"}` to the last `input_text` block of the re-sent history: the 400 above.
- `prompt_cache_key`: no difference, as the guide says for 5.6+.
- For comparison, codex-cli 0.160.1 itself reads cache only for its pre-warmed fixed opening part (12,032 tokens per call). A repeated user block was not read back on a second call.

### Expected

The backend accepts `prompt_cache_breakpoint` for gpt-6.1-sol, as the public Responses API documents, so a multi-turn session reads its earlier turns from cache.

### Related

#35300 (the Codex client cannot emit the field). With a breakpoint added by hand, that report measured 0% → 98.6% cache hits on a stable 9k-token prefix, but the backend has to accept it first.

# Separate configuration and discovery deadlines in workspace routing

The 0.160.0 resolver starts its discovery deadline before managed configuration
loading and post-discovery configuration reloading finish. A configuration delay
can therefore exhaust the discovery budget even when discovery itself completes
promptly, and a reload failure can be reported as a discovery timeout.

A synthetic reproduction uses a fresh configuration getter for every load:

1. Return the initial configuration immediately and complete discovery promptly.
2. Delay the first post-discovery configuration reload for sixteen seconds.
3. Observe whether that reload can complete under its own thirty-second budget,
   rather than failing at the fifteen-second discovery deadline.

Two additional controls delay reload beyond its own budget, and cancel startup
while reload is pending. They distinguish a configuration timeout from a discovery
timeout and verify that shutdown remains cancellation-responsive. The production
constructor should also populate the routing cache through its actual detached
startup task without a second explicit request.

The proposed correction bounds configuration phases separately, starts the
discovery budget around discovery itself, and retains origin, override, cache,
and cancellation behavior. With identical synthetic reload controls, the corrected
source passes all three cases while the original production source fails them.

This report describes source-level reproduction. It does not establish a repaired
signed desktop runtime, deployed behavior, or complete regression-suite coverage.
